method: For each of the 30 holdout items: (1) mcp__wiki-mcp__kb_search(query=item.question, limit=10, multi_query=false, use_v1=true) -- identical call to baseline-A; (2) take the #1-ranked search hit's document id as the sole graph anchor (no retry with a different anchor, no manual anchor curation); (3) mcp__wiki-mcp__kb_graph_explore(anchor_type='document', anchor_value=<top hit id>); (4) merged candidate set = search top-10 ids union first-10 graph '연관 문서' ids, dedup, first-occurrence order preserved; (5) check whether any of the item's frozen candidate_documents ids appears in that merged set, and at what position; classify found_by_search_alone / found_by_graph_only / found_by_neither / no_anchor_available. Recall/rank is strict exact-id matching against holdout-2026-10-14.json, no substitution.
anchor_reuse_note: When the same document id recurred as the #1 search hit across multiple items, the previously-fetched kb_graph_explore result was reused instead of re-calling the tool, to avoid redundant identical calls. Reused anchors: confluence_docs:2306565544 (middleware-02, network-04, network-06, network-07, openstack-02), confluence_docs:2498030568 (network-09, network-10), confluence_docs:1880429955 (vmware-02, windows-01), confluence_docs:1836189018 (linux-01, performance-04). This does not change any classification -- a reused anchor's result set was already known to contain no match against any holdout candidate seen so far, including the new item's candidates.
methodology_caveat: Tool-call counts (30 kb_search + 22 actual kb_graph_explore calls, 8 anchor-reuses) are exact and reliable. Wall-clock latency was NOT consistently bracketed with per-item timestamps for this measurement -- this fork's execution was interrupted mid-run by a context-compaction event, and on resumption the remaining ~18 items were processed without re-instrumenting per-item date+%s%N timestamps (tool-call counts, not timing, were the priority to recover cleanly). The two timestamps that do exist from this run (middleware-02 ~16087ms, middleware-03 ~120665ms) are not representative: middleware-03's bracket incidentally includes an unrelated large file re-read forced by the context-compaction recovery, so it is excluded from any latency statistic entirely. Given this gap, no credible combined-path p50/p95 is reported here; see 'latency' section below for what can honestly be said.

tool_calls.note: mean_additional = actual graph_explore calls / 30 items; reuse optimization cut what would otherwise be a flat 1.0 extra call/item down to 0.733

latency.reason_not_reported: Per-item wall-clock timestamps were not consistently captured across this measurement run (a mid-run context-compaction event interrupted instrumentation; see methodology_caveat). Reporting a p50/p95 built from a handful of surviving, non-uniformly-collected samples would imply a precision this data does not have. The one usable sample (middleware-02, found_by_neither, anchor reused) was ~16087ms for the combined search+graph_explore pair, in the same order of magnitude as baseline-A's search-only p50 of ~10928ms, consistent with the graph step adding roughly one more tool round-trip's worth of latency on top of search -- but this is a single data point, not a distribution.
latency.qualitative_cost_estimate: Structurally, the combined path costs exactly 1 extra MCP call (kb_graph_explore) per item versus baseline-A's search-only path, except where anchor-reuse applies (8/30 items here), where it costs 0 extra calls. A clean re-measurement with per-item timestamps from the first call onward would be needed for a trustworthy p50/p95 of the combined path.

found_by_graph_only_examples_note: Zero items were rescued by the graph step across all 30 holdout questions. Every item classified as a hit (13/30) was already found by kb_search alone at or above rank 8; every item kb_search missed (17/30) also had its naive top-1-search-hit anchor lead to a kb_graph_explore result with no overlap against that item's frozen candidate_documents. In every found_by_neither case the anchor was either an isolated/near-empty node (0-5 related docs: network-01, network-11's small cluster, database-01/vmware-01's isolated status) or a generic high-degree 'hub' node (1124 to 15089 related documents, typically PISA checkitems connected through extremely common inferred components such as filesystem, hang, ESXi, MTU, HANA, A10, L4/L7) whose neighbor set never contains the specific incident report being searched for.
qualitative_findings: This naive graph-augmentation strategy (anchor = kb_search's #1 hit, no re-ranking or relevance filtering of the anchor itself) shows zero measured recall or MRR benefit over search alone on this holdout: recall_at_merged_set and MRR are identical to baseline-A to four decimal places, because the merged candidate set never gained a hit that search didn't already have. This directly informs F06 ranking-design scope: adding a raw 2-hop graph traversal keyed on the top search result is not sufficient on its own to justify its added tool-call cost; a smarter anchor-selection strategy (e.g. requiring a minimum search-score threshold before trusting the anchor, or anchoring on multiple top-k hits rather than just rank 1) would need to be designed and separately measured before graph augmentation could be expected to pay for itself.

The failure mode is bimodal and anchor-quality-driven, not graph-size-driven: isolated/tiny-neighborhood anchors (network-01, network-11, database-01, vmware-01) simply have nothing nearby to find, while large hub anchors (3000-15000+ neighbor docs, recurring across unrelated items because the same generic inferred components -- filesystem, hang, ESXi, A10, L4/L7, MTU, HANA -- dominate the graph) are too undifferentiated to surface the one relevant document among thousands of generic PISA checkitems. Both failure modes stem from the same root cause: the #1 kb_search hit for these natural-language paraphrased questions is usually only weakly related to the actual incident (scores ~0.015-0.028), so the graph is being asked to extend from an already-weak signal.

Three new found_by_neither items (performance-01, kubernetes-01 already noted in baseline-A, and this run's storage-02 confirmation) repeat the cross-source-type near-miss pattern: a topically-correct document exists in the corpus for the exact same real-world event, but under a different source_type/document_id than the one the holdout froze as ground truth (performance-01's CITECTS-2534 ticket vs. its incident_reports id; kubernetes-01's CITECTS-2594 ticket vs. its incident_reports id; storage-02's tech_repo/1932298856 NetApp-encryption-key-sync doc vs. its incident_reports id). This is unaffected by adding graph traversal and remains purely an exact-id-matching artifact relevant to F05's namespace/identity-domain discussion, not a graph or ranking finding per se.
